newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-POLYGRAM SEES FLAT OR LOWER 1996.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-POLYGRAM SEES FLAT OR LOWER 1996.

text.p: PolyGram NV said on Wednesday its 1996 operating profits would be flat or slightly below 1995 because of lower than expected music sales.
The recorded music and film company -- 75 percent owned by Philips Electronics NV -- said it would take a $90 million reorganisation charge against its 1996 results.

"Entering the important fourth quarter the company currently expects the full-year 1996 operating result before restructuring charges to be flat or slightly below last year's, caused by lower than expected music sales," PolyGram said in a statement.
The restructuring will involve the rejuvenation of Motown, the black U.S. pop label acquired in 1993, its classical music division and distribution and marketing operations in Europe.
PolyGram said it had fallen victim to sluggish music markets worldwide but added that music sales were also lower than expected due to problems within PolyGram itself.

The company's shares fell sharply on the Amsterdam bourse as investors were disappointed by the prospect of a second year of flat profit growth. In 1995 PolyGram posted a net profit of 741 million guilders ($431 million), almost unchanged from 738 million in 1994.

By 1100 GMT PolyGram shares were off 6.20 guilders at 78.70. In London the shares of EMI Group Plc fell 22 pence to 1,258 in sympathy with PolyGram, after earlier slumping to 1,238.5 -- a low since its demerger from the former Thorn EMI.
PolyGram spokeswoman Amanda Conroy said the rejuvenation of Motown was a key goal of the planned restructuring.

"Management is taking positive steps to...make sure that the (Motown) label rejuvenates itself with new artists," she said. "It has a fantastic back catalogue, obviously, but any record label needs to bring on new artists."
PolyGram said it was making management changes at Motown and overhauling its artist and repertoire department that is responsible for signing new talent.
Conroy said PolyGram was also taking action to offset the effects of several years of flat sales in the market for recordings of classical music.
"The way we're addressing this problem at PolyGram is to revamp our three classical labels -- Decca, Deutsche Grammophon, Philips Classics," she said.
"We've reinvigorated the management at PolyGram Classics and with their input we'll be changing the focus and direction and where necessary the organisation of our global classical music business."
Conroy said PolyGram could not make any comment about its likely financial results for 1997 at this stage.
